vulnerabilities.title: STACK_BUFFER_OVERFLOW — read() writes 0x80 bytes into 0x68-byte buffer, overwriting canary, saved RBP, and return address

root_cause.description: vuln_func allocates a stack frame of 0x70 bytes (sub rsp,0x70). The input buffer starts at [rbp-0x70] and the stack canary is stored at [rbp-0x8], leaving 0x68=104 bytes of usable buffer space before the canary. However, read() is called with a count of 0x80=128 bytes (mov edx,0x80), which writes 0x80 bytes starting at [rbp-0x70]. This overflows by 0x18=24 bytes past the canary, covering: 8 bytes of stack canary at [rbp-0x8], 8 bytes of saved RBP at [rbp], and 8 bytes of return address at [rbp+0x8]. The return address IS directly reachable by a single read of 0x80 bytes. The root cause is a size mismatch: the read count (0x80) exceeds the buffer capacity (0x68 before canary), with no bounds check on the read length.

affected_objects: stack buffer at [rbp-0x70] (0x68 bytes usable before canary)

data_flow: stdin → read(0, [rbp-0x70], 0x80) at 0x1254 (first read) and 0x1284 (loop read)
canary check at 0x12a1-0x12ae: XOR [rbp-0x8] with fs:0x28; if mismatch → __stack_chk_fail
if canary intact: leave; ret uses overwritten return address at [rbp+0x8]

security_check.expected: read() count should not exceed buffer capacity (0x68 bytes before canary), or buffer should be large enough to hold 0x80 bytes
security_check.actual: read() is called with count=0x80 (128 bytes) into a buffer with only 0x68 (104) bytes of space before the canary — no bounds check on read length vs buffer size
security_check.missing_or_incorrect: No validation that the read count (0x80) fits within the allocated buffer space (0x68). The read count exceeds the buffer capacity by 24 bytes, overwriting the canary, saved RBP, and return address.

vulnerable_operation.target: stack buffer [rbp-0x70], overflow into [rbp-0x8] (canary), [rbp] (saved RBP), [rbp+0x8] (return address)
vulnerable_operation.size: 0x80=128 bytes written into 0x68=104-byte buffer space, 24-byte overflow

impact.reason: Attacker-controlled 128-byte input overwrites 24 bytes past the buffer: 8 bytes of stack canary, 8 bytes of saved RBP, and 8 bytes of return address. This corrupts the stack frame's integrity metadata and control-flow data. The return address at [rbp+0x8] is directly overwritten by bytes 0x78-0x7f of the input.

If the overwritten canary value does not match fs:0x28, __stack_chk_fail is called at 0x12b0, terminating the process. If the canary is correctly reproduced (e.g., via leak from BUG-002) and the return address is overwritten with an invalid value, a SIGSEGV occurs on ret.

evidence.description: sub rsp,0x70 allocates 0x70=112 bytes of stack frame. Buffer at [rbp-0x70] starts at the bottom of the frame.
Stack canary loaded from fs:0x28 and stored at [rbp-0x8]. Buffer space from [rbp-0x70] to [rbp-0x8] is 0x68=104 bytes.

mov edx,0x80 sets read count to 128 bytes. Buffer at [rbp-0x70] has only 0x68=104 bytes before canary. Overflow = 0x80-0x68 = 0x18=24 bytes, covering canary (8B at [rbp-0x8]), saved RBP (8B at [rbp]), and return address (8B at [rbp+0x8]).
Second read in loop also uses mov edx,0x80 — same overflow occurs on every loop iteration, allowing repeated overwrite attempts.

Canary check at exit: mov rax,[rbp-0x8]; xor rax,fs:0x28; je 0x12b5; call __stack_chk_fail. If canary is corrupted, __stack_chk_fail aborts. If canary is preserved (e.g., via leak), leave;ret executes with overwritten saved RBP and return address at [rbp+0x8].

verification_required: Confirm that read() does not NUL-terminate the buffer, enabling the puts() leak in BUG-002 to recover the canary value
Confirm that sending exactly 0x80 bytes in a single read overwrites the return address at [rbp+0x8]
Confirm whether the canary's NUL byte (low byte on x86-64) can be leaked byte-by-byte via repeated puts() calls with partial fills

vulnerabilities.title: STACK_INFORMATION_LEAK — puts(buf) echoes non-NUL-terminated buffer, leaking stack canary and adjacent stack data

root_cause.description: vuln_func calls puts(buf) at 0x1262 to echo user input back to stdout. The read() call at 0x1254/0x1284 does NOT NUL-terminate the input — read() returns raw bytes without appending a NUL. puts() reads from the buffer start until it encounters a NUL byte (0x00). If the user sends input that fills the buffer without a NUL terminator, puts() will read past the user's data into adjacent stack memory, including the stack canary at [rbp-0x8] and potentially saved RBP at [rbp]. The stack canary on x86-64 Linux has its lowest byte (first in memory due to little-endian) set to 0x00, which acts as a natural NUL terminator — but the bytes above it (canary bytes 1-7) can still be leaked if the user fills exactly up to the canary boundary. Additionally, on subsequent loop iterations, if the user sends fewer bytes than the previous iteration, residual data from prior reads remains in the buffer and can be leaked by puts().

attack_surface.input: stdin via read(fd=0, buf=[rbp-0x70], count=0x80), echoed via puts(buf)
data_flow: Attacker sends N bytes via stdin (N < 0x68, no NUL terminator)
read(0, [rbp-0x70], 0x80) writes N bytes to buffer, does NOT append NUL
puts([rbp-0x70]) at 0x1262 reads from buffer start until first NUL byte
If no NUL in first N bytes, puts reads into bytes N..0x67 (residual/uninitialized stack data)
If no NUL before [rbp-0x8], puts reads canary bytes — stopped by canary's NUL low byte
Canary bytes 1-7 leaked to stdout, enabling canary reconstruction for BUG-001 bypass

security_check.expected: Buffer should be NUL-terminated before passing to puts(), or a length-bounded output function should be used
security_check.actual: read() does not NUL-terminate; puts() reads until NUL with no length bound — if user input lacks NUL, puts reads past user data into stack canary and adjacent memory
security_check.missing_or_incorrect: No NUL-termination of the buffer after read(). No use of length-bounded output (e.g., fwrite with explicit length). puts() relies on a NUL terminator that read() does not guarantee.

vulnerable_operation.target: stack buffer and adjacent stack memory (canary at [rbp-0x8], saved RBP at [rbp])
vulnerable_operation.size: unbounded — reads until first NUL byte in memory starting at [rbp-0x70]

impact.reason: puts(buf) outputs buffer contents until NUL. Since read() does not NUL-terminate, and the buffer may contain residual data from prior iterations or uninitialized stack content, puts() can leak stack memory beyond the user's input. Critically, if the user fills the buffer up to the canary boundary (0x68 bytes without NUL), puts() will read into the canary at [rbp-0x8]. The canary's low byte is 0x00 (NUL), so puts stops there — but the 7 non-NUL canary bytes above it are leaked to stdout. This enables canary recovery, which is a precondition for exploiting BUG-001 (the stack overflow that overwrites the return address).

evidence.description: read(0, [rbp-0x70], 0x80) — read() syscall does not NUL-terminate the buffer. The buffer content after the read is raw input bytes with no guaranteed NUL.

puts([rbp-0x70]) — puts() reads from [rbp-0x70] until the first NUL byte, then outputs all those bytes plus a newline. If no NUL exists in the user's input, puts reads into adjacent stack memory (canary at [rbp-0x8], saved RBP at [rbp]).

The loop structure (puts → puts('Input:') → read → strcmp → jne loop) allows multiple iterations. On each iteration, if the user sends fewer bytes than the buffer size, residual data from previous reads remains. This enables byte-by-byte probing: send N bytes (no NUL), observe puts output length to detect where NUL bytes exist in adjacent stack memory, gradually reconstruct the canary value.

Stack canary from fs:0x28 stored at [rbp-0x8]. On x86-64 Linux, the canary's least significant byte (first in memory at [rbp-0x8] due to little-endian) is 0x00. This NUL byte stops puts() from reading further, but the 7 bytes at [rbp-0x7] through [rbp-0x1] (canary bytes 1-7) are leaked if the user fills the buffer to [rbp-0x8] without a NUL.

verification_required: Confirm dynamically that read() does not NUL-terminate the buffer and that puts() leaks bytes beyond user input
Confirm that the canary's low byte is 0x00 and that bytes 1-7 can be leaked via puts() when buffer is filled to the canary boundary
Confirm that the loop allows iterative byte-by-byte canary reconstruction via partial fills and puts() output length observation

non_vulnerabilities.description: init() calls setvbuf(stdout, NULL, _IONBF, 0) to disable buffering and alarm(60) to set a 60-second timeout. These are standard setup calls with no security implications.
non_vulnerabilities.reason: setvbuf parameters are correct (unbuffered stdout). alarm(60) limits process lifetime but does not introduce a vulnerability. No user-controlled data flows into these calls.

non_vulnerabilities.description: main() calls init() then vuln_func() and returns 0. No direct user input processing in main itself.
non_vulnerabilities.reason: main is a simple dispatcher — all user input handling is delegated to vuln_func. No vulnerability in main's own logic.

non_vulnerabilities.description: The strcmp(buf, "--") comparison at 0x1297 controls loop exit. An attacker can control how many loop iterations occur by sending non-'--' input.
non_vulnerabilities.reason: While the attacker controls loop iteration count, this is by design (echo service). The loop itself is not a vulnerability — it is an enabler for BUG-001 and BUG-002 (multiple read/puts cycles for canary leak and repeated overflow attempts). The strcmp comparison is correct (full string comparison, not partial).

non_vulnerabilities.function: vuln_func — read() return value not checked
non_vulnerabilities.description: The return value of read() (number of bytes actually read) is not checked or used. The code proceeds to puts(buf) and strcmp(buf, "--") regardless of how many bytes were read.
non_vulnerabilities.reason: While not checking read()'s return value is a minor robustness issue, it does not introduce a security vulnerability in this context. The buffer overflow (BUG-001) exists regardless of whether the return value is checked, because the count parameter (0x80) is the limiting factor, not the actual bytes read. The info leak (BUG-002) depends on the absence of NUL termination, not on the return value.

unresolved.description: Whether the canary can be fully reconstructed via the puts() leak to bypass the stack canary protection for BUG-001
unresolved.reason: The canary's low byte is 0x00 (NUL), which stops puts() from reading past it. The 7 high bytes can be leaked. However, the low byte is always 0x00, so the full 8-byte canary can be reconstructed as 0x00 || leaked_7_bytes. This needs dynamic confirmation of the exact leak behavior.
unresolved.required_next_step: S3 should dynamically verify: (1) send 0x68 bytes without NUL, observe if puts() output contains 7 canary bytes; (2) confirm canary low byte is 0x00; (3) confirm the reconstructed canary value allows bypassing the __stack_chk_fail check when used in BUG-001's overflow.

unresolved.description: Whether the return address overwrite in BUG-001 can be combined with the canary leak from BUG-002 to achieve control-flow corruption
unresolved.reason: BUG-001 overwrites the return address at [rbp+0x8] (bytes 0x78-0x7f of the 0x80-byte read). BUG-002 can potentially leak the canary. If the canary is leaked and correctly placed in the overflow payload, __stack_chk_fail is not triggered, and the overwritten return address takes effect on ret. This combined attack path needs dynamic verification.
unresolved.required_next_step: S3 should dynamically verify the combined attack: (1) leak canary via BUG-002, (2) construct 0x80-byte payload with correct canary at offset 0x68 and desired return address at offset 0x78, (3) send via read() in the loop, (4) send '--' to exit loop and trigger ret with overwritten return address.

unresolved.description: S1 fact F010 incorrectly states the return address is NOT directly reachable
unresolved.reason: S1 fact F010 claims 'Return address at [rbp+0x8] is NOT directly overwritten by a single 0x80 read.' However, the buffer starts at [rbp-0x70] and read writes 0x80=128 bytes, reaching [rbp-0x70+0x80]=[rbp+0x10]. The return address at [rbp+0x8] falls within this range (bytes 0x78-0x7f of the read). S1 appears to have miscalculated the buffer size as 0x70 (the full frame) rather than 0x68 (frame minus canary slot). The return address IS directly reachable.
